column1: # 29장 말투 지시(11-10). 열: 조각 앞머리 → 지시(영어, 짧게). @scene 행은 장면 설명. 윤하의 "Vale."(두 번)와 "Sí."는 앞머리가 겹쳐 지시하지 않는다.
@scene 십일월 이십일 금요일 아침 일곱 시
column2: Friday, November 20, seven in the morning, still dark. Marc, the reserved locksmith, picks Yuna up in the workshop van to drive her to the airport, with Montse and Vale. Vale, the young Argentine lodger, now mixes her Argentine "che" with the Spanish "tío" (mate, dude) that she picked up in Barcelona; Montse calls that a crime against two countries. Quiet morning, light teasing over sadness.

column1: 십일월 이십일 금요일 아침 일곱 시

column2: sleepy complaint; "tío" is new Spanish slang for her

column1: Ya sé, tío. Era un comentario, che.
column2: breezy; mixing "tío" and "che" in one sentence

column1: @scene Salimos de Gràcia por calles vacías.
column2: The drive to the airport at dawn. Yuna remembers arriving three and a half months ago with five words, not knowing what "vale" meant. Now she lists what vale, venga and tío really mean in people's mouths. Reflective, tender, a little proud.

column1: Salimos de Gràcia por calles vacías.

column2: tender, a small smile, savouring each word
quiet, brief; "venga" here means "come on, we're here"

column1: @scene En el mostrador, la chica de la aerolínea
column2: Check-in at El Prat. Yuna understands every question from the airline clerk and asks for a window seat for the return flight, to see Barcelona when she lands. Then Montse, who has barely spoken, gives her a small parcel for her mother: the postcard Yuna's grandmother sent her, on loan. Montse says she never says "adiós" to people she wants back, only "hasta luego". Quietly emotional.
easy and natural, she understands now

column1: Para tu madre. Ábrelo con ella.
La postal. La de tu abuela.
column2: tender, voice almost breaking; "Es prestada" a loving, firm joke

column1: Te la traigo. Te lo prometo.

column2: whispered in her ear, first in Catalan then Spanish; stress "adiós" and "hasta luego"
moved, choosing the words on purpose

Goodbyes at security. Vale hugs Yuna, half crying, threatening her if she doesn't come back. They trade "Vale" (Spain's "okay") and "Dale" (the Argentine "okay") back and forth like a game. Then Marc gives Yuna his grandfather's wristwatch, set to Barcelona time, and kisses her. They say "hasta luego", not goodbye. Bittersweet, restrained.
laughing and crying at once, Rioplatense; mock threats

column1: Es el mío. Bueno, era de mi abuelo.
column2: low and plain, a bit shy

column1: Sí puedes. Para que cuentes los días.
¿Y tú qué reloj vas a llevar?
Tengo uno muy grande en el sótano.
column2: dry, a smile in his voice
his voice a little strange, holding back
low, a promise; the date and time said carefully

column1: @scene 보안 검색대를 지나 한 번 뒤를 돌아보았다
column2: Yuna looks back once at Montse, Vale and Marc behind the glass. At passport control a young police officer asks if she lives here; she realizes her home is now in Gràcia. He answers kindly, "hasta luego, vecina" (neighbour). Quietly happy.

column1: 보안 검색대를 지나 한 번 뒤를 돌아보았다
Sí. Bueno… a ver a mi madre.

column2: thinking, then sure and warm; "mi casa está en Gràcia" quietly proud

On the plane. Yuna orders easily in Spanish, remembering that in August she could only say "sí, gracias". Barcelona shrinks below. She looks at Marc's watch on Barcelona time and, as in August, writes words on her palm. Quiet, bittersweet, at peace.

column1: Un café con leche, por favor.
El avión despegó hacia el mar
